description: I'm a 4th-​year Civil Engineering student from the Philippines with experience in GIS/spatial analysis, environmental and water-resources research, Python, data analysis, statistics, and basic ML. I'm interested in Earth observation, remote sensing, and environmental monitoring. Looking for teammates in SAR, Python, web development, visualization, UI/UX, or Earth science. Starting independently and open to collaborators.
summary:
NISAR Surface Change Monitor is an interactive desktop app that shows how the ground surface of Sarangani and Davao Occidental in Mindanao, Philippines is changing. These two provinces were hit by an M7.8 earthquake on 8 June 2026 and now face an El Niño season.

Answering the Dancing with the SARs challenge, the app turns NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar into map layers that are easy to read: backscatter by pass and by month, month-to-month change, radar-estimated vegetation, and 2020–2026 land-cover change. It puts these alongside Landsat HLS, MODIS, GPM IMERG and SRTM layers for post-earthquake landslide screening, El Niño time series, and a 12-month drought outlook.

This matters because local planners and responders need surface-change information they can trust without radar expertise. Every value in the app traces back to a pinned data release, and the app states clearly what the data cannot show.
details:
The app opens in 3D on the two provinces, on NISAR's own map of trees and plants. A left panel has four topics, each with a few simple maps. Picking a map shows one map at a time, with bullet notes, the satellite used, the dates and a colour scale:

  1. Space radar (NISAR): trees and plants (HV), wet ground (HH), September→October change, an AI greenness map made from radar, and 2026 land types from radar.
  2. Earthquake: the 305 possible landslides after the 8 June 2026 M7.8 quake, coloured by whether NISAR confirms them, plus the epicentre, steep slopes and a Sentinel-1 radar cross-check.
  3. El Niño: NISAR soil wetness before and after the dry spell, with MODIS and Landsat greenness, heat, leaf water and surface water.
  4. The Next 12 Months: a NISAR "watch first" map, plus scenario maps of browning, chance of browning, heat, and places that dry first.

Anyone can tap a spot to read values, compare dates, play the timeline, bookmark places and download data. A desktop version (Tauri) works offline.

Why NISAR: the cloud problem

Southern Mindanao is cloudy most of the year. On the dates NISAR passed over in 2026, Landsat had a clear view of only 0.5–62% of the same ground within ±8 days — on 25 September, 0.5%. NISAR's 24 cm radar waves pass through cloud and into the forest canopy.

We used 8 NISAR L2 GCOV pass dates (28 June – 19 October 2026). A single pass covers 19–89% of the area. Averaging every pass in a month (in power, not dB) gives complete maps for September and October. Gaps are left blank, never filled with guesses.

How we did the science

We wrote down testable hypotheses, tested each against a control, and report the ones that failed as well as the ones that passed.

H1. NISAR can confirm earthquake landslides through clouds.

  • Landsat HLS found 305 possible landslide patches (165 ha) after the 8 June quake: steep slopes (≥20°) whose greenness (EVI) dropped from ≥0.35 to ≤0.20, by at least 0.25 more than the normal 2025 seasonal change. Two thirds are around Glan and Jose Abad Santos. Our 165 ha is close to the PhilSA estimate of about 138 ha.
  • NISAR, a completely independent sensor, sees the same spots as 2.86 dB darker in HV than other steep land (95% bootstrap CI −3.02 to −2.66 dB). HV darkens when there is less leaf and branch volume.
  • Compared like with like, the gap holds within every land-cover class (−2.2 to −3.3 dB) and every slope band (−2.8 to −3.1 dB).
  • 194 of 305 patches (64%) fall in the darkest quarter of steep land, where chance would give 25%.

H2. Shorter C-band radar (Sentinel-1) can do the same.

  • Our teammate Alfie Pelicano processed 7 Sentinel-1 interferometry pairs on two tracks, including pre-quake control pairs.
  • The coherence drop at the spots matched other steep land: 0.024 vs 0.025, and 0.000 vs −0.003.
  • Over dense tropical vegetation, Sentinel-1 coherence was already at noise level before the quake (above 0.5 at only 9% and 2% of spots). This null result shows why NISAR's longer L-band wavelength matters here.

H3. NISAR tracks the land drying and re-wetting through El Niño.

  • GPM rainfall over the provinces fell to 17% of normal in August 2026 and 44% in September, then recovered to 79% in October.
  • From September to October, NISAR HH backscatter, which responds to soil moisture, rose by more than 1 dB on 32% of the land and fell on 10%.
  • It rose most where soil is exposed (annual crops 48%, grassland 40%) and least under closed forest (28%), as radar physics predicts.

H4. El Niño strength predicts the coming dry season.

  • Nov–Apr rainfall since 1998 follows the El Niño index (ONI): r = −0.81. Tested on each year left out of training: r = 0.83, mean error 138 mm (28 years).
  • Each MODIS pixel gets its own model on 2000–2026 data: anomaly = a + b·ONI + c·(September–October anomaly), after removing its seasonal cycle and trend.
  • Under the NOAA-forecast strong El Niño (ONI +2.5 °C, range +2.0 to +3.0), Nov 2026 – Apr 2027 rain is expected at 41% of normal (341 vs 825 mm). Browning peaks in April 2027 with a 78% chance of below-normal greenness. This is a scenario, not a forecast.

H5. AI can turn NISAR into a greenness map under clouds.

  • Gradient-boosted trees were trained on 167,858 pixels where NISAR and Landsat saw the ground within 8 days, and scored on 210 held-out 5 km blocks, so they are never tested next to their training pixels.
  • NISAR + terrain explains R² = 0.37 of greenness (EVI); NISAR alone 0.24, terrain alone 0.12 — most of the skill comes from NISAR.
  • A NISAR land-cover map agrees with the 2020 national map at 63% (κ 0.57). We present these as patterns, not field-level values.

From science to action: the "watch first" map. We combine the places the El Niño model says will lose the most greenness (worst third) with the places where NISAR already sees thin plant cover (thinnest third). Together they cover 15% of the land (~770 km²), mainly the Maasim lowlands and the Glan–Jose Abad Santos coast. NISAR repeats every 12 days, so this list can be updated every month.

Uncertainty and what we do not claim

NISAR data is provisional and starts after the quake; the landslides are not field-checked; the outlook is a scenario. The table shows each limit and how we handled it.

Data

Six NASA datasets plus partner data, all free and open. All processed layers, scripts and figures are in our open data release; the science write-up has scripts that reproduce every chart and number above. Every map in the app records which source file it came from.

Benefits

  • Local disaster offices (MDRRMO, PDRRMO): a free map of where slopes failed and where vegetation is already thin before the El Niño dry season, with its evidence and limits, updated with every NISAR pass.
  • Farmers and agricultural offices: which farm areas dried most in the dry spell, and which may brown first in early 2027.
  • Everyone: simple language, one map at a time, a colour scale on every map, and every number traceable to open NASA data.

What we hope to achieve

  • Show that NISAR can serve as a monthly, cloud-proof monitor for small, cloudy, disaster-prone provinces.
    • field-check the landslide spots with the local DRRM offices
    • add the June 2026 NISAR passes and pre-quake data as ASF releases them
    • update the watch list automatically as new NISAR passes arrive

Tools we used

  • Analysis: Python (NumPy, rasterio/GDAL, scikit-learn HistGradientBoosting, matplotlib), QGIS, NASA AppEEARS and GIOVANNI, ASF Vertex and HyP3.
  • App: React + TypeScript, MapLibre GL JS (3D terrain), Vite, Tauri (desktop), Astro Starlight (docs), Cloudflare R2 (map tiles), GitHub Pages and GitHub Actions (tests and builds).
